title: Stage 1: a bounded queue and a worker pool
summary: Jobs go into a bounded channel; a pool of workers runs them; a full queue says no in time; a failing job is counted, never fatal.

steps.title: The brief
body: Every service grows one: a place to put work that should not run inside the request. Sending e-mails, rendering thumbnails,
calling a slow partner. You will build it in three stages, the way it grows at work.
record Job(string Id, string Tenant, string Payload);
record PipelineOptions(int Capacity, int Workers, TimeSpan EnqueueWait);
class Pipeline(PipelineOptions options, Func<Job, CancellationToken, Task> handle)
public void Start(CancellationToken stopping);                         // start options.Workers workers
public ValueTask<bool> TryEnqueueAsync(Job job, CancellationToken ct); // false if still full after EnqueueWait
public Task StopAsync(TimeSpan drainTimeout);                          // no more jobs; let the workers finish the queue
public int Processed { get; }                                           // jobs whose handler returned
public int Failed { get; }                                              // jobs whose handler threw
The tests are deterministic: handlers wait on gates the tests open, so "is the queue full?" and "how many run at once?" have exact
answers. `System.Threading.Channels` and `System.Collections.Concurrent` are imported for you.

steps.prompt: Capacity 2, one worker, and its handler is stuck on the first job. How many `TryEnqueueAsync` calls in a row return `true` before one returns `false`?
options: 3: one taken by the worker, two waiting in the channel
All of them: the channel grows
steps.explain: Once the worker has read the first job, it is out of the channel. The channel then holds two more, and the fourth write waits until `EnqueueWait` runs out.

steps.prompt: Match each part of the pipeline to the tool from the course.
pairs: `try`/`catch` per job inside the worker loop

steps.title: Build the pipeline
prompt: Write `Job`, `PipelineOptions` and `Pipeline` as in the brief:
- `Start` launches `options.Workers` workers that read jobs and `await handle(job, token)`, one at a time each;
- `TryEnqueueAsync` waits at most `options.EnqueueWait` for room and returns `false` if there is none (a cancelled `ct` throws);
- a handler that throws increments `Failed`; one that returns increments `Processed`; the worker goes on either way;
- `StopAsync` completes the channel and waits for the workers to finish everything already queued.
**Run checks** runs the tests: everything processed, at most `Workers` at once, a full queue says no, failures counted.

solution: record Job(string Id, string Tenant, string Payload);
record PipelineOptions(int Capacity, int Workers, TimeSpan EnqueueWait);
class Pipeline(PipelineOptions options, Func<Job, CancellationToken, Task> handle)
public async ValueTask<bool> TryEnqueueAsync(Job job, CancellationToken ct)
catch (Exception e) when (e is not OperationCanceledException || !stopping.IsCancellationRequested)
template: static async Task Until(Func<bool> ok) { for (var i = 0; i < 200 && !ok(); i++) await Task.Delay(10); }
await Dojo.TryAsync("Every job runs once", async () =>
var p = new Pipeline(new PipelineOptions(4, 3, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)), async (job, ct) => { await Task.Yield(); seen.Add(job.Id); });
for (var i = 0; i < 20; i++) await p.TryEnqueueAsync(new Job($"j{i}", "t1", "x"), CancellationToken.None);
Dojo.Eq("StopAsync waits until all 20 jobs ran", 20, p.Processed);
Dojo.Eq("Each job ran exactly once", 20, seen.Count);
await Dojo.TryAsync("Workers run in parallel, never more than options.Workers", async () =>
var p = new Pipeline(new PipelineOptions(10, 3, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)), async (job, ct) =>
for (var i = 0; i < 6; i++) await p.TryEnqueueAsync(new Job($"j{i}", "t1", "x"), CancellationToken.None);
Dojo.Eq("Three workers busy at once", 3, Volatile.Read(ref inFlight));
await Dojo.TryAsync("A full queue says no in time", async () =>
var p = new Pipeline(new PipelineOptions(2, 1, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(30)), async (job, ct) => { started.TrySetResult(); await gate.Task; });
Dojo.Check("Job 1 accepted", await p.TryEnqueueAsync(new Job("j1", "t1", "x"), CancellationToken.None), "");
Dojo.Check("Jobs 2 and 3 fill the queue", await p.TryEnqueueAsync(new Job("j2", "t1", "x"), CancellationToken.None)
&& await p.TryEnqueueAsync(new Job("j3", "t1", "x"), CancellationToken.None), "With capacity 2 and job 1 taken by the worker, two more fit.");
Dojo.Check("Job 4 is refused after EnqueueWait", !await p.TryEnqueueAsync(new Job("j4", "t1", "x"), CancellationToken.None),
"The queue is full: TryEnqueueAsync must give up after EnqueueWait and return false.");
Dojo.Eq("The three accepted jobs ran", 3, p.Processed);
await Dojo.TryAsync("A failing job is counted and the worker goes on", async () =>
var p = new Pipeline(new PipelineOptions(4, 1, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)), async (job, ct) =>
foreach (var payload in new[] { "ok", "boom", "ok" }) await p.TryEnqueueAsync(new Job(payload, "t1", payload), CancellationToken.None);
static void InterlockedMax(ref int target, int value)
var actual = Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref target, value, seen);
hints: Start from `Channel.CreateBounded<Job>(new BoundedChannelOptions(options.Capacity) { FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait })`. Workers: `Task.Run(() => WorkAsync(stopping))`, kept in an array for `StopAsync`.
`TryEnqueueAsync`: a linked `CancellationTokenSource` with `CancelAfter(options.EnqueueWait)`; catch `OperationCanceledException` `when (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)` and return false.
`StopAsync`: `_queue.Writer.TryComplete(); await Task.WhenAll(_workers);`. In the worker, wrap each handler call in try/catch and count with `Interlocked`.
explain: This is already more robust than most hand-rolled queues: bounded memory, backpressure the caller can turn into a 503, failures
isolated per job. Stage 2 makes it stop cleanly.
